title: Workflow orchestration vs choreography
description: Learn the difference between orchestration and choreography for coordinating distributed workflows. Understand when to use centralized vs decentralized coordination.

data.text: Orchestration and choreography are two approaches to coordinating workflows across multiple services. Orchestration uses a central coordinator, while choreography lets services coordinate themselves through events.
Orchestration uses a central coordinator service that manages the entire workflow, telling each service when to execute its part.

items: Central coordinator defines the workflow logic
Coordinator calls services in the correct order
Coordinator handles failures and retries
Single place to understand the workflow
Coordinator becomes a single point of complexity

data.title: Analogy
data.text: Orchestration is like a conductor leading an orchestra. The conductor decides when each instrument plays and coordinates the performance.
Choreography lets services coordinate themselves through events. Each service knows when to act based on events it receives from other services.

items: Services emit events when they complete work
Services listen for events to know when to act
No central coordinator—decentralized logic
Each service contains part of the workflow logic
Harder to understand the overall workflow

data.title: Analogy
data.text: Choreography is like dancers performing without a conductor. Each dancer knows their moves and responds to the other dancers' movements.

items.title: Orchestration
items.description: Centralized control, easier to understand workflow, coordinator is a bottleneck, better for complex workflows, single point of failure.

items.title: Choreography
items.description: Decentralized control, harder to understand overall flow, no single bottleneck, better for simple workflows, more resilient.

items: Complex workflows with many steps
When you need central visibility and control
When the workflow logic changes frequently
When you need to handle complex failure scenarios
When you want to minimize workflow logic in services
Simple workflows with few steps
When you want decentralized control
When services are loosely coupled
When you want to avoid a single coordinator
When the workflow is unlikely to change

data.title: Hybrid Approach
data.text: Many systems use both: orchestration for complex workflows, choreography for simple event-driven interactions.

items: Orchestration: Use workflow engines like Temporal, Airflow, or AWS Step Functions
Choreography: Use event buses like Kafka, AWS EventBridge, or RabbitMQ
Monitor workflow execution in both approaches
Document the workflow logic clearly
Test failure scenarios thoroughly
Orchestration: More control, more complexity in coordinator
Choreography: Less control, complexity distributed across services
Orchestration: Easier to reason about, single point of failure
Choreography: Harder to reason about, more resilient
